mcqs.question: You want a regularizer that tends to push some feature weights to exactly zero, effectively selecting features. Which norm should the penalty use?
options: L2, because it penalizes large weights the most
L1, because its constant gradient magnitude keeps pushing small weights all the way to zero
L∞, because it only cares about the single largest weight
Any norm works identically for feature selection
mcqs.explanation: L1's penalty grows linearly, so its gradient has constant magnitude even as a weight shrinks — it keeps pushing weights to exactly zero (Lasso). L2's gradient shrinks with the weight, so it shrinks weights smoothly but rarely to exact zero. L∞ only bounds the worst coordinate and isn't used for sparsity.

mcqs.question: Two document embeddings point in nearly the same direction, but one document is much longer, giving it a much larger vector magnitude. Which metric treats them as most similar?
options: Euclidean distance, since it accounts for the difference in length
Cosine similarity, since it ignores magnitude and compares direction only
Both metrics give the same ranking in every case
Neither metric can be used when vectors differ in magnitude
mcqs.explanation: Cosine similarity normalizes out magnitude and compares only the angle between vectors, so two documents about the same topic score as similar regardless of length. Euclidean distance would penalize the longer document for simply having larger coordinate values, which is the wrong signal for topical similarity.

mcqs.question: In a regression model, two input features are near-perfect linear combinations of each other. What's the practical symptom?
options: The model simply ignores one of the two features automatically
Training becomes unstable and coefficient estimates blow up or swing wildly with small data changes
The features become orthogonal to each other automatically
Nothing changes — linear independence only matters for classification, not regression
mcqs.explanation: Near-linear-dependence (multicollinearity) makes the underlying matrix nearly singular, so the least-squares solution becomes ill-conditioned: small changes in data cause large, unstable swings in the fitted coefficients. The model doesn't detect and drop the redundant feature on its own — that's a separate step like regularization or feature selection.
